entry_json.definition: a period of time when a teacher teaches a group of students
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have an English lesson every Tuesday evening after work.
example_sentences: Our first lesson starts at nine in the morning.
She gives private lessons to students who want to take IELTS.

entry_json.definition: to allow someone to do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My parents let me choose my own university course.
example_sentences: The teacher let us leave ten minutes early.
Please let me know if the time does not suit you.

confusables.difference: Let is followed by a verb with no to: let me go. Allow needs to: allow me to go. Allow is also more formal, so use it in writing.

entry_json.avoid: Never say let me to go. After let, the next verb takes no to.

entry_json.definition: a message that you write on paper and send to someone by post; also one of the signs a, b, c that we use to write words
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I wrote a letter to the college asking about their evening courses.
example_sentences: The word bandready has ten letters.
In IELTS Writing Task 1 for the General test, you write a letter.

entry_json.definition: how high or how much something is, or how good someone is at something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My level of English improved a lot once I started speaking every day.
example_sentences: Sea levels are rising in many parts of the world.
Students are placed in classes according to their level.

entry_json.definition: a building or room where books are kept for people to read or borrow
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I do most of my studying in the university library because my flat is noisy.
example_sentences: The city library opens at eight and closes at ten.
You can borrow up to six books from the library at a time.

confusables.difference: In a library you borrow books and give them back. In a bookshop you buy them and keep them.

entry_json.definition: the time when a person is alive, or the way a person lives
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Life in a big city is faster than life in the village where I grew up.
example_sentences: City life offers more jobs but costs more money.
He has lived in the same town all his life.
entry_json.avoid: The plural is lives, not lifes.

entry_json.definition: the way a person lives, for example how they work, eat and spend free time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A healthy lifestyle means more than just going to the gym twice a week.
example_sentences: Many young people now have a very busy lifestyle.
Sitting all day is part of a modern office lifestyle.

entry_json.definition: a machine that carries people up and down inside a tall building
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The lift in our building was broken, so I walked up eight floors.
example_sentences: Take the lift to the third floor and turn left.
There is no lift in the old library, only stairs.
collocations: a lift to the top floor

confusables.difference: Lift is British English, elevator is American English. The IELTS examiner accepts both, but keep one style through the whole answer.

entry_json.definition: probably going to happen or probably true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is likely that more people will work from home in the future.
example_sentences: Heavy rain is likely later this week.
Students who read widely are more likely to do well in the exam.

confusables.difference: Likely is an adjective: it is likely that prices will rise. Probably is an adverb: prices will probably rise. Do not say it will likely happen in formal writing.

entry_json.definition: a long thin mark, or a row of people or things one behind the other
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There was a long line of people waiting outside the ticket office.
example_sentences: Draw a straight line under the title.
The graph shows a clear upward line after 2010.

entry_json.definition: a way that two things are joined, or a word or picture on a website that takes you to another page
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Researchers have found a clear link between sleep and memory.
example_sentences: There is a strong link between air quality and public health.
I sent you a link to the course timetable.

entry_json.definition: a large wild cat with yellow-brown hair that lives in Africa and parts of Asia
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We saw three lions resting under a tree on the safari.
example_sentences: Lions are losing their natural home as farms grow larger.
The zoo has two young lions.

entry_json.definition: a group of names or things that you write one under another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I keep a list of new words on my phone and read it on the bus.
example_sentences: Make a list of everything you need to buy.
Her name was not on the list of successful candidates.

entry_json.definition: to pay attention to a sound so that you can hear it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I listen to the news in English every morning while I make breakfast.
example_sentences: Listen carefully to the recording before you answer.
He never listens to advice from his teachers.

confusables.difference: Listen is something you choose to do; hear just happens. I listened to the recording twice but I could not hear the last word.

entry_json.avoid: Listen needs to before its object: listen to the radio, not listen the radio.

entry_json.definition: a person who listens, especially to the radio or to another person speaking
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A good listener does not interrupt while the other person is speaking.
example_sentences: The programme has over a million listeners.
My sister is a very patient listener.

entry_json.definition: belonging to the small area near where you live
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I do my shopping at the local market rather than the supermarket.
example_sentences: The local council is planning a new cycle path.
Tourists should try the local food.

entry_json.definition: to close something with a key so that other people cannot open it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Please lock the door when you leave the classroom.
example_sentences: I locked my bike to the railing outside the library.
She forgot to lock the window before going away.

entry_json.definition: to turn your eyes towards something because you want to see it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Look at the graph and describe the main changes.
example_sentences: She looked out of the window at the rain.
You look tired this morning.

confusables.difference: Look is what you do on purpose; see is what your eyes do anyway. I looked at the chart for a minute before I saw the pattern.
You watch something that moves or changes over time: watch a film, watch a match. You look at something still: look at a photo.

entry_json.avoid: Look needs at before an object: look at the picture, not look the picture.

entry_json.definition: a large road vehicle used for carrying heavy things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Heavy lorries are not allowed in the town centre during the day.
example_sentences: A lorry blocked the road for almost an hour.
Most goods in this country are still moved by lorry.

confusables.difference: Lorry is British English and truck is American English. They mean the same vehicle.

entry_json.definition: to no longer have something, because you cannot find it or someone took it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I lost my student card during the first week of term.
example_sentences: Many people lose their jobs when a factory closes.
Our team lost the match by one goal.

confusables.difference: Lose is a verb and rhymes with news. Loose is an adjective meaning not tight, and rhymes with juice. Do not write I might loose my job.

entry_json.avoid: The past forms are lost, not losed.

entry_json.definition: not knowing where you are, or not able to be found
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I got lost on my first day and arrived twenty minutes late.
example_sentences: The lost luggage was returned to her two days later.
We got lost trying to find the exam centre.

entry_json.definition: a large amount or a large number
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a lot of traffic in my city between eight and nine.
example_sentences: A lot of students work part time while they study.
I learned a lot from that course.

confusables.difference: A lot of works with both countable and uncountable nouns in any sentence. Much is mainly used in questions and negatives: I do not have much time.

entry_json.avoid: In formal Task 2 writing, prefer many, a great deal of or a significant number of instead of a lot of.

entry_json.definition: making a lot of noise
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The music in the cafe was so loud that we could not talk.
example_sentences: There was a loud noise from the building site next door.
Her voice is loud enough for the whole room to hear.

entry_json.definition: in a way that makes a lot of noise
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The group behind us was talking loudly through the whole film.
example_sentences: He knocked loudly on the door.
She laughed loudly at the joke.

entry_json.definition: to like someone or something very much
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I love cooking at the weekend because it helps me relax.
example_sentences: She loves her job even though the hours are long.
I would love to visit Japan one day.
entry_json.avoid: Love is not normally used in the continuous form: say I love this city, not I am loving this city.

entry_json.definition: very nice or very beautiful
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We had a lovely afternoon walking along the river.
example_sentences: That is a lovely photo of your family.
The weather was lovely all week.
entry_json.avoid: Lovely sounds warm and friendly, so it fits Speaking Part 1. In Task 2 writing choose a more neutral word such as pleasant or attractive.

entry_json.definition: not high, or not much in amount
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wages in that industry are low, so young people leave the area.
example_sentences: The country has a low birth rate.
Keep your voice low in the reading room.

entry_json.definition: good or bad things that happen to you by chance and not because of what you did
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Finding a flat so close to the campus was pure luck.
example_sentences: Good luck with your exam tomorrow.
We had no luck finding a cheap ticket.
entry_json.avoid: Luck is uncountable: say a piece of luck or some luck, never a luck.

entry_json.definition: having good things happen to you by chance
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was lucky to get a place on the course at such short notice.
example_sentences: We were lucky with the weather on our trip.
She feels lucky to have such supportive parents.

entry_json.definition: a meal that you eat in the middle of the day
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I usually have lunch at my desk to save time.
example_sentences: We had lunch in a small cafe near the station.
Lunch is served between twelve and two.
entry_json.avoid: Do not use a before meals in general statements: have lunch, not have a lunch.

entry_json.definition: a piece of equipment with moving parts that does a job for people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The factory bought new machines and needed fewer workers.
example_sentences: A washing machine saves several hours a week.
Machines now do many jobs that people used to do.

entry_json.definition: a thin book with a paper cover, full of articles and pictures, that comes out every week or month
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I read a science magazine on the train to keep up with new research.
example_sentences: She writes for a travel magazine.
Print magazines are losing readers to websites.

entry_json.definition: letters and parcels that are sent and brought to your home or office
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The mail arrives at about eight every morning.
example_sentences: Your passport will be sent by mail.
I checked my mail before leaving the house.

confusables.difference: These sound the same but mail means letters and parcels, and male means a man or a boy. Only the spelling shows the difference.
In British English, post is the more common word for letters delivered to your door. Mail is used more in American English, and in both for email.

entry_json.definition: largest or most important
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main reason I chose this city was the cost of living.
example_sentences: The main problem is a lack of affordable housing.
Our main office is in the city centre.

entry_json.definition: very large or very important
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Traffic is a major problem in almost every growing city.
example_sentences: The government has announced a major change to the tax system.
Cost is a major factor when students choose a university.

confusables.difference: Main picks out the single most important one: the main reason. Major just means large or serious, and there can be several: three major problems.

entry_json.definition: to produce something, or to cause something to happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I make a plan every Sunday for what I will study that week.
example_sentences: Studying abroad made me much more independent.
The company makes parts for electric cars.

confusables.difference: Make is for creating or producing a result: make a cake, make a decision, make progress. Do is for actions and work in general: do homework, do the washing up, do research. You make a mistake, but you do an exercise.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say make homework or make a research. Those take do.

entry_json.definition: being a man or a boy, or an animal that does not give birth to babies
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chart shows that male students outnumber female students on engineering courses.
example_sentences: Both male and female workers reported the same problem.
The male bird has brighter feathers.

confusables.difference: Male is about sex; mail is letters and parcels. They sound identical, so check the spelling in writing.

entry_json.definition: an adult male person
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The man sitting next to me on the flight was a teacher from Spain.
example_sentences: A young man asked me for directions to the station.
Two men were repairing the road outside.
entry_json.avoid: The plural is men, with a different vowel sound: mæn becomes men.

entry_json.definition: to succeed in doing something difficult, or to control the work of a group of people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I managed to finish the essay the night before the deadline.
example_sentences: She manages a team of twelve people.
We managed to find a flat within our budget.

confusables.difference: Manage to always means there was a difficulty and you got past it. Can just means you have the ability. I can swim, but I managed to swim across the lake.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to control the work of other people or of a business
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My manager lets us work from home two days a week.
example_sentences: She was promoted to branch manager last year.
A good manager listens to the team before deciding.

entry_json.definition: the way that something is done, or the way a person behaves towards others
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She explained the rules in a friendly manner, so nobody felt nervous.
example_sentences: The doctor spoke to the patient in a calm manner.
Please complete the form in the manner shown in the example.
entry_json.avoid: Manners with an s means polite behaviour: good table manners. Manner without an s means the way something is done.

entry_json.definition: a drawing of an area that shows roads, rivers, towns and other features
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The map shows the same town centre in 1990 and today.
example_sentences: I used a paper map because there was no phone signal.
Look at the map and find the shortest route to the station.

entry_json.definition: a number or letter that a teacher gives to show how good a piece of work is; also a small dirty area or line on something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I got a good mark for my essay but a lower one for the speaking test.
example_sentences: The pass mark for the course is fifty out of a hundred.
There was a dirty mark on the wall near the door.

confusables.difference: A mark is usually a number, such as 68. A grade is usually a letter or band, such as A or B. British schools often use mark, American schools use grade.

entry_json.definition: a place where people meet to buy and sell things, often outside; also the buying and selling of a product in general
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a street market near my flat every Saturday morning.
example_sentences: Fruit is much cheaper at the market than in the supermarket.
The job market for young graduates has become harder.

entry_json.definition: having a husband or a wife
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My sister has been married for six years and lives near my parents.
example_sentences: He got married last summer in a small ceremony.
Married couples can apply for the family discount.
entry_json.avoid: You get married to someone, not get married with someone.

entry_json.definition: to become the husband or wife of someone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: They decided to marry after finishing their studies.
example_sentences: She married a colleague she met at work.
In many countries people marry later than they used to.
entry_json.avoid: Marry takes a direct object with no preposition: he married her, not he married with her.

entry_json.definition: what something is made of, such as wood, metal or glass; also information you use for study
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chairs are made of recycled material, which keeps the price low.
example_sentences: Building materials have become much more expensive.
The teacher gave us extra reading material for the exam.

entry_json.definition: the study of numbers, shapes and sizes
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Mathematics was my strongest subject at school.
example_sentences: She has a degree in mathematics from a local university.
Mathematics is taught in every year of secondary school.

confusables.difference: Mathematics is the full, formal word and fits written English. Maths is the short British form used in speech. The American short form is math.

entry_json.avoid: Although it ends in s, mathematics takes a singular verb: mathematics is difficult.

entry_json.definition: the short everyday word for mathematics, the study of numbers and shapes
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had a maths lesson every day at secondary school.
example_sentences: My brother is much better at maths than I am.
She teaches maths to teenagers.

confusables.difference: Maths is British English and math is American English. Both are short for mathematics. Keep to one form in your answer.

entry_json.definition: a subject or situation that you have to think about or deal with
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The cost of housing is a serious matter for young families.
example_sentences: This is a matter for the local council, not the government.
It is only a matter of time before the price rises again.
entry_json.avoid: What is the matter? means what is wrong. It is a fixed question, not a general use of matter.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something is possible but you are not sure
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Maybe I will study abroad next year, but it depends on the cost.
example_sentences: Maybe fifty people came to the talk.
Maybe we should leave earlier to avoid the traffic.

confusables.difference: They mean the same, but maybe is more informal and usually starts a sentence in speech. Perhaps sounds better in Task 2 writing.
Maybe as one word is an adverb: maybe he is late. May be as two words is a verb: he may be late. Both are correct but they are not interchangeable.

entry_json.avoid: In formal writing, prefer perhaps, possibly or it is possible that.

entry_json.definition: the word you use to talk about yourself when you are not the person doing the action
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My tutor gave me some useful advice about the writing test.
example_sentences: Could you send me the timetable, please?
She sat next to me during the exam.

confusables.difference: I does the action: I called her. Me receives it or follows a preposition: she called me, between you and me. Say she and I went, not she and me went.

entry_json.definition: the food that you eat at one time, such as breakfast, lunch or dinner
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I try to cook one proper meal a day instead of buying fast food.
example_sentences: The price includes three meals a day.
A hot meal after a long journey makes a real difference.

entry_json.definition: to have a particular sense, or to plan to do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Living in the city centre means I can walk to work.
example_sentences: What does this word mean in the passage?
I did not mean to interrupt you.
entry_json.avoid: To ask about a word, say what does it mean, not what means it.

entry_json.definition: what a word, sign or action tells you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I looked up the meaning of the word before using it in my essay.
example_sentences: The same word can have several meanings.
Try to guess the meaning from the words around it.

entry_json.definition: food that comes from the body of an animal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I eat meat only twice a week to reduce my impact on the environment.
example_sentences: Producing meat uses far more water than growing vegetables.
She does not eat meat or fish.

confusables.difference: These sound the same. Meat is food; meet is to come together with someone. Watch the spelling in writing.

entry_json.avoid: Meat is uncountable: say some meat or a piece of meat, not a meat.

entry_json.definition: television, radio, newspapers and the internet, seen together as a way of giving news to people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The media report bad news far more often than good news.
example_sentences: Social media has changed how young people get their information.
The story was covered by media all over the world.
entry_json.avoid: The media is normally used with the: the media, not just media.

entry_json.definition: connected with doctors, hospitals and helping people who are ill
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Free medical care is one of the main reasons people support the system.
example_sentences: She is studying for a medical degree.
Employees can get medical treatment through the company scheme.

confusables.difference: Medical is the adjective: medical care. Medicine is the noun: the pills themselves, or the subject doctors study.

entry_json.definition: something you take to make you better when you are ill; also the study and work of doctors
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I take this medicine twice a day until the course is finished.
example_sentences: The chemist gave me some medicine for my cough.
He studied medicine for six years before becoming a doctor.
entry_json.avoid: You take medicine; you do not eat or drink it.

entry_json.definition: to come together with someone at the same place, or to see someone for the first time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I met my best friend on the first day of university.
example_sentences: Let us meet outside the library at two.
The committee meets once a month.
collocations: meet someone for the first time

confusables.difference: Meet someone is the normal British form. Meet with is more American and suggests a planned business discussion.

entry_json.avoid: The past form is met, not meeted.

entry_json.definition: a time when people come together to talk about something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We have a short team meeting every Monday morning.
example_sentences: The meeting was moved to Thursday afternoon.
She could not attend the meeting because of a train delay.

entry_json.definition: a person who belongs to a group, club or organization
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have been a member of the university running club for two years.
example_sentences: Members pay a lower price for tickets.
Each member of the family had a different opinion.

entry_json.definition: the ability to remember things, or something that you remember
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My memory for names is poor, so I write them down.
example_sentences: Regular sleep improves memory and concentration.
I have happy memories of my school years.

entry_json.definition: to say or write something about someone or something, without giving many details
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report mentions air pollution but does not explain the causes.
example_sentences: She mentioned that she was thinking of moving abroad.
Did the teacher mention the deadline?
entry_json.avoid: Do not put to after mention before the thing: he mentioned the problem, not he mentioned to the problem.

entry_json.definition: a list of the food you can order in a restaurant; also a list of choices on a screen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The restaurant has a short menu but everything on it is fresh.
example_sentences: Could we see the menu, please?
Open the settings menu and choose your language.

entry_json.definition: words that you write or say and send to someone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I sent my tutor a message asking for an extra week.
example_sentences: Leave a message and I will call you back.
The advertisement carries a clear message about road safety.

entry_json.definition: a hard material such as iron, steel or gold, used to make cars, keys and coins
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The frame is made of light metal, so the chair is easy to carry.
example_sentences: Metal can be recycled again and again without losing quality.
The bridge is built from steel and other metals.

entry_json.definition: a particular way of doing something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Repeating words out loud is the method that works best for me.
example_sentences: Traditional teaching methods are still used in many schools.
The researchers explain their method in the second section.

confusables.difference: Way is the everyday word and fits speaking: the best way to learn. Method sounds more formal and organized, so it suits Task 2 and academic writing.

entry_json.definition: a unit we use to say how long something is; one metre is one hundred centimetres
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The new bridge is about two hundred metres long.
example_sentences: The room is four metres wide.
Sea levels could rise by almost a metre this century.

confusables.difference: In British English, metre is the length and meter is a machine that measures, such as a gas meter. American English spells both meter.

entry_json.definition: the part of something that is the same distance from all its sides or ends
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a small park in the middle of the city.
example_sentences: I woke up in the middle of the night.
Put the table in the middle of the room.

confusables.difference: Centre is the exact point and is used for places and organizations: the city centre, a sports centre. Middle is looser and works for time as well: the middle of the week.

entry_json.definition: twelve o clock at night
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The library closes at midnight during the exam period.
example_sentences: Our train arrived just after midnight.
The offer ends at midnight on Sunday.
entry_json.avoid: Use at with midnight and no article: at midnight, not in the midnight.

entry_json.definition: a unit we use to say how far something is; one mile is about one point six kilometres
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I live about three miles from the campus, so I cycle in.
example_sentences: The nearest hospital is ten miles away.
Britain still measures road distances in miles.

entry_json.definition: the white drink that comes from cows
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have milk in my tea but not in my coffee.
example_sentences: Could you buy a bottle of milk on your way home?
Milk production uses a large amount of land and water.
entry_json.avoid: Milk is uncountable: a bottle of milk or some milk, not a milk.

entry_json.definition: the part of you that thinks, remembers and feels
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I changed my mind about the course after speaking to a graduate.
example_sentences: Keep an open mind when you read the argument on the other side.
The idea stayed in my mind for weeks.

entry_json.definition: a piece of special glass that you can see yourself in
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a large mirror by the door so people can check their appearance.
example_sentences: She looked in the mirror before the interview.
The mirror makes the small room look bigger.

entry_json.definition: to fail to catch or attend something, or to feel sad because someone is not with you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I missed the first bus and arrived late for the lecture.
example_sentences: He missed two lessons because he was ill.
I miss my family more than I expected.
entry_json.avoid: After miss, the next verb ends in ing: I missed seeing her, not I missed to see her.

entry_json.definition: not in the place where it should be, and not able to be found
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Two pages were missing from the exam paper, so we were given extra time.
example_sentences: The report says a key figure is missing from the table.
My umbrella has been missing since Tuesday.

entry_json.definition: something you do or think that is wrong
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My biggest mistake was leaving the essay until the last night.
example_sentences: There are three spelling mistakes in this paragraph.
It was a mistake to travel without booking a room.

confusables.difference: A mistake is the wrong thing you did. A fault is who is to blame or a weakness in something: it was my fault, or a fault in the machine.

entry_json.avoid: You make a mistake. Do not say do a mistake.

entry_json.definition: able to be moved or carried around easily
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Almost everyone here has a mobile phone, even in small villages.
example_sentences: The clinic uses a mobile unit to reach remote villages.
Mobile internet has replaced fixed lines for many users.

confusables.difference: British English says mobile or mobile phone; American English says cell phone. The IELTS listening test uses the British form.

entry_json.definition: used to describe verbs such as can, must and should, which show ability, need or how sure we are
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Using modal verbs such as may and might makes an argument sound more careful.
example_sentences: Can, could and should are all modal verbs.
A modal verb is followed by the base form: she must go.
entry_json.avoid: After a modal verb, use the base form with no to: he can swim, not he can to swim.

entry_json.definition: a small copy of something, or a good example that others can follow
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The museum has a model of the old city as it looked in 1800.
example_sentences: Finland is often used as a model for school reform.
He built a model of the bridge for his engineering project.

entry_json.definition: of the present time, or using the newest ideas and methods
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Modern life leaves many people with very little free time.
example_sentences: The hospital uses modern equipment donated last year.
Modern buildings often use more glass than brick.

confusables.difference: New just means recently made: a new car. Modern means it belongs to the present age and its way of doing things: modern architecture. A new building can be built in an old style.

entry_json.definition: a very short period of time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: For a moment I could not remember the word I needed.
example_sentences: Could you wait a moment while I check the timetable?
At the moment I am living with my parents to save money.
entry_json.avoid: At the moment means now. Do not confuse it with in a moment, which means soon.

entry_json.definition: what people use to pay for the things they buy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I try to save a little money each month for travel.
example_sentences: Students often spend most of their money on rent.
The charity raised money for a new school.
entry_json.avoid: Money is uncountable: much money, some money, a lot of money. Never say moneys or a money.

entry_json.definition: a small animal with a long tail that lives in trees in hot countries
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Monkeys near the temple often take food from visitors.
example_sentences: We saw a group of monkeys beside the road.
Monkeys are losing their habitat as forests are cut down.

entry_json.definition: one of the twelve parts of a year
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I pay my rent at the start of every month.
example_sentences: The course lasts six months.
Last month was the wettest on record.

entry_json.definition: the big bright object in the sky at night that moves around the Earth
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The moon was so bright that we could walk without a torch.
example_sentences: Humans first landed on the moon in 1969.
The moon affects the tides in the sea.
entry_json.avoid: Use the with moon when you mean our moon: the moon, not a moon.

entry_json.definition: a larger amount or number of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: More people are choosing to work from home than ten years ago.
example_sentences: I need more time to finish the report.
This city has more parks than the one where I grew up.

confusables.difference: More compares two things: this city is more crowded than that one. Most picks the top of three or more: this is the most crowded city in the country.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use more with an adjective that already ends in er: say cheaper, not more cheaper.

entry_json.definition: the early part of the day, from when the sun comes up until twelve o clock
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I study best in the morning before anyone else is awake.
example_sentences: The exam starts at nine in the morning.
She goes running every morning before work.
entry_json.avoid: Say in the morning, but on Monday morning. The preposition changes when a day is named.

entry_json.definition: almost all of something, or most of the time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My course is mostly online, with one class on campus each week.
example_sentences: The audience was mostly students.
We mostly eat at home because restaurants are expensive.

confusables.difference: Most goes with a noun: most students. Mostly is an adverb and goes with a verb or a whole idea: the group was mostly students.

entry_json.definition: a female parent
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My mother taught me to cook when I was about twelve.
example_sentences: Working mothers often need affordable childcare.
She looks very like her mother.

entry_json.definition: a vehicle with two wheels and an engine
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A motorcycle is cheaper than a car and easier to park in the city.
example_sentences: He rides a motorcycle to work in all weathers.
Motorcycle riders must wear a helmet by law.

confusables.difference: They mean the same vehicle. Motorbike is the everyday spoken word in Britain; motorcycle sounds more formal and appears in written rules.

entry_json.definition: a very high hill with sides that go up quickly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We spent the weekend walking in the mountains north of the city.
example_sentences: The mountain is covered in snow until late spring.
Climbing that mountain takes two days.

confusables.difference: A hill is much lower and easier to walk up. A mountain is high and steep, usually over about six hundred metres.

entry_json.definition: a small grey animal with soft hair that lives in houses and fields; also the small thing you move with your hand to control a computer
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My computer mouse stopped working in the middle of the test.
example_sentences: A mouse got into the kitchen through a gap in the door.
Click the right button on the mouse to open the menu.
entry_json.avoid: The animal plural is mice. For the computer device, both mice and mouses are used, but mice is safer.

entry_json.definition: the part of your face that you use for eating and speaking
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cover your mouth when you cough so that you do not spread germs.
example_sentences: He opened his mouth to reply but said nothing.
The dentist asked me to open my mouth wide.

entry_json.definition: to change position or to go to live in a different place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We moved to a smaller flat to reduce our rent.
example_sentences: Could you move your bag so I can sit down?
Many young people move to the capital to find work.

entry_json.definition: the act of changing position, or a group of people working for the same change
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chart shows the movement of goods between the two ports.
example_sentences: The environmental movement has grown quickly among young people.
Sensors record every movement of the machine.

entry_json.definition: a story shown as moving pictures at a cinema or on a screen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We watched an old movie at home instead of going out.
example_sentences: The movie was based on a true story.
Streaming has changed the way people watch movies.

confusables.difference: They mean the same thing. Film is the usual British word and sounds more formal; movie is American and more casual. IELTS accepts either.

entry_json.definition: the informal word for mother
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I call my mum every Sunday evening.
example_sentences: My mum still lives in the house where I grew up.
Mum, have you seen my keys?

confusables.difference: Mum is warm and informal and belongs in Speaking Part 1. Mother is neutral and is the safer choice in writing. American English uses mom.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use mum in Task 2 writing. Write mother or parents.

entry_json.definition: a building where old and interesting things are kept for people to see
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The city museum is free, so I take visitors there every time.
example_sentences: The museum has a large collection of local photographs.
Many museums now offer online tours.

entry_json.definition: the sounds you make when you sing or play an instrument, put together so that they are good to hear
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I listen to quiet music while I revise because it helps me concentrate.
example_sentences: Live music brings a lot of visitors to the city each summer.
She has played music since she was six.
entry_json.avoid: Music is uncountable: some music or a piece of music, never a music.

entry_json.definition: connected with music, or good at playing or singing music
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Learning a musical instrument as a child improves concentration later.
example_sentences: She comes from a very musical family.
The school lends musical instruments to students who cannot buy one.

entry_json.definition: a person who plays a musical instrument or writes music, often as a job
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Street musicians play outside the station every Friday evening.
example_sentences: Many musicians now earn more from concerts than from recordings.
He is a professional musician as well as a teacher.

entry_json.definition: belonging to me
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My first language is Tamil, but I studied in English from the age of ten.
example_sentences: My flat is a ten minute walk from the station.
I left my notes on the train.

confusables.difference: My comes before a noun: my book. Mine stands alone: that book is mine. Never say my is the red one.

entry_json.definition: used when the person doing the action and the person receiving it are both you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I taught myself to cook using videos online.
example_sentences: I cut myself while chopping vegetables.
I did the whole project myself.

confusables.difference: Use myself only when I is also the subject: I helped myself. If someone else does the action, use me: she helped me. Do not say please contact myself.

entry_json.definition: the word or words that a person or thing is called
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Please write your full name in capital letters at the top of the form.
example_sentences: I am sorry, I have forgotten your name.
The street takes its name from an old factory.

entry_json.definition: small in distance from one side to the other
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The old streets are too narrow for buses to pass.
example_sentences: We walked along a narrow path beside the river.
The gap between rich and poor is not narrow at all.

confusables.difference: Narrow is about width from side to side: a narrow road. Thin is about thickness or about a person who is not fat: a thin book, a thin man.

entry_json.definition: connected with a whole country
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Public transport here is run at national rather than city level.
example_sentences: The national newspaper reported the story on its front page.
Health care is funded from the national budget.

confusables.difference: National covers the whole country; local covers only the small area around you. A national policy applies everywhere, a local one only in that town.

entry_json.definition: made by nature and not by people; or normal and not surprising
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The island still has large areas of natural forest.
example_sentences: Wind and sunlight are natural sources of energy.
It is natural to feel nervous before a speaking test.

entry_json.definition: all the plants, animals and land that were not made by people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Spending time in nature is one of the cheapest ways to reduce stress.
example_sentences: Children who grow up near nature tend to be more active.
Human activity is changing nature faster than ever before.
entry_json.avoid: When you mean the natural world, use nature without the: in nature, not in the nature.

entry_json.definition: a short distance from someone or something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I live near the university, so I walk to my lectures.
example_sentences: There is a good bakery near the station.
Do not sit near the door if you feel cold.
entry_json.avoid: Near needs no to: near the station, not near to the station in everyday use.

entry_json.definition: almost, but not completely
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Nearly half the students in my class come from another country.
example_sentences: I have nearly finished the report.
It took nearly three hours to get there.

confusables.difference: Near is about distance: I live near the park. Nearly means almost and goes with a number, verb or adjective: nearly ten, nearly ready.

entry_json.definition: needed in order for something to happen or to be done
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is necessary to book the exam at least a month in advance.
example_sentences: A visa is necessary for citizens of most countries.
Make only the changes that are strictly necessary.
entry_json.avoid: Say it is necessary to do something or it is necessary that you do something. Do not say it is necessary you to do.

entry_json.definition: the part of the body that joins the head to the shoulders
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Sitting at a screen all day has given me a stiff neck.
example_sentences: He hurt his neck playing football.
Wrap a scarf around your neck in cold weather.

entry_json.definition: to have to have something because it is important or necessary
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I need a quiet place to study in the evenings.
example_sentences: You need to arrive thirty minutes before the test.
The city needs more affordable housing.

confusables.difference: Need means something is necessary; want means you would like it. I need water to live, but I want coffee.

entry_json.avoid: Say I need to go, not I need go.

entry_json.definition: bad or not helpful, or saying no
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Working night shifts had a negative effect on my health.
example_sentences: Too much screen time has a negative impact on sleep.
Her answer was negative, so the plan was dropped.

confusables.difference: They are opposites. A positive effect helps, a negative effect harms. In grammar, a negative sentence uses not.

entry_json.definition: a person who lives next to you or very near you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My neighbour keeps a spare key in case I lock myself out.
example_sentences: We invited our new neighbours for dinner.
Good neighbours make a street feel safe.

confusables.difference: Neighbour is the British spelling and neighbor is American. IELTS accepts both, but do not mix spellings in one answer.

entry_json.definition: worried or a little afraid about something that is going to happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was nervous before the speaking test, but the examiner was friendly.
example_sentences: She gets nervous when she has to speak in front of a group.
There is no reason to be nervous about the interview.
entry_json.avoid: Use nervous about, not nervous for: nervous about the exam.

entry_json.definition: a group of things or people that are connected to each other
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The city has an excellent network of cycle paths.
example_sentences: A good rail network reduces the number of cars on the road.
She built a network of contacts during her first job.

entry_json.definition: not at any time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have never travelled outside my own country.
example_sentences: She never eats breakfast before work.
I will never forget my first day at university.
entry_json.avoid: Never is already negative. Do not add not: say I never go, not I do not never go.

entry_json.definition: made or bought a short time ago, or not known before now
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I started a new job in September and I am still learning the systems.
example_sentences: The city opened a new library last year.
Learning a new language takes patience.

entry_json.definition: information about things that have just happened
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I check the news on my phone while I wait for the bus.
example_sentences: The news about the factory closing spread quickly.
She watches the news every evening at six.
entry_json.avoid: News is uncountable and takes a singular verb: the news is good, not the news are good. Say a piece of news, never a news.

entry_json.definition: large sheets of paper with the news on them, sold every day or every week
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandfather still buys a newspaper every morning.
example_sentences: Newspaper sales have fallen sharply since people started reading online.
The story appeared on the front page of every newspaper.

entry_json.definition: coming immediately after this one in time or order
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am taking the exam next month, so I study every evening.

Turn left at the next set of traffic lights.
entry_json.avoid: Do not use in or on before next week or next year: I will start next week, not in next week.

entry_json.definition: good, and easy to like
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It was nice to meet people from so many different countries.
example_sentences: We had a nice walk along the beach.
My neighbours are very nice to me.

entry_json.definition: the dark part of the day, when most people sleep
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I find it hard to sleep at night when the street outside is noisy.
example_sentences: Nurses who work at night often have poor sleep.
We stayed two nights in a small hotel.
entry_json.avoid: Say at night for nights in general, but on Friday night when the day is named.

entry_json.definition: used to give a negative answer, or to mean not any
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is no easy answer to the housing problem.
example_sentences: No, I have not been to that museum yet.

confusables.difference: No goes before a noun: there is no time. Not makes a verb negative: there is not enough time. Do not say there is not time.

entry_json.definition: not one person
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Nobody in my family had been to university before me.

entry_json.avoid: Nobody is already negative and takes a singular verb: nobody knows, not nobody do not know.

entry_json.definition: a sound, especially one that is loud or that you do not like
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The noise from the main road makes it hard to sleep with the window open.

There was a strange noise coming from the engine.

confusables.difference: Sound is neutral and covers anything you can hear: the sound of rain. Noise is usually unwanted or too loud: the noise of building work.

entry_json.definition: making a lot of loud sound that people do not like
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My flat is cheap but very noisy because it faces the main street.

Noisy machinery can damage hearing over time.

entry_json.definition: usual, ordinary and what you expect
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is normal to feel tired in the first weeks of a new job.
example_sentences: Trains returned to their normal times after the strike.
A normal working week here is thirty seven hours.

entry_json.definition: usually, or in the way that people expect
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I normally get up at six, but at weekends I sleep longer.
example_sentences: The office is normally closed on Saturdays.
Normally the journey takes half an hour.

confusables.difference: They are very close in meaning. Normally slightly suggests what is standard or correct; usually simply reports how often. Either fits Speaking Part 1.

entry_json.definition: the direction that is on your left when you look at the rising sun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I grew up in the north of the country, where the winters are long.
example_sentences: The wind was coming from the north.
Manchester lies in the north west of England.
entry_json.avoid: Use in the north of a country you are inside, and to the north of something you are outside.

entry_json.definition: the part of your face that you use for breathing and smelling
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The cold air made my nose run all the way to the station.
example_sentences: He broke his nose playing rugby.
Breathe in slowly through your nose.

entry_json.definition: used to make a word, phrase or sentence negative
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I do not agree that money is the most important thing in a job.
example_sentences: The library is not open on Sundays.
She is not interested in politics.

entry_json.definition: a short piece of writing that helps you remember something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I take notes in every lecture and read them again the same evening.
example_sentences: She left a note on the kitchen table.
Make a note of the reference number.

entry_json.definition: not one thing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is nothing wrong with asking the examiner to repeat a question.
example_sentences: I had nothing to eat before the test.
Nothing changed after the meeting.
entry_json.avoid: Nothing is already negative: say I know nothing or I do not know anything, never I do not know nothing.

entry_json.definition: to see or hear something and know that it is there
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I noticed a mistake in my essay only after I had handed it in.
example_sentences: Did you notice how quiet the street was this morning?
Nobody noticed that the sign had been changed.
entry_json.avoid: After notice, use a bare verb or an ing form: I noticed him leave or I noticed him leaving, not I noticed him to leave.

entry_json.definition: at this time, or at this moment

example_sentences: Prices are much higher now than five years ago.
We should leave now or we will miss the train.

entry_json.definition: in no place, or to no place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is nowhere to park near the hospital, which frustrates visitors.

entry_json.avoid: Nowhere is already negative: say there is nowhere to sit, not there is not nowhere to sit.

entry_json.definition: a word or sign such as two or seven that shows how many there are
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The number of students choosing science has risen every year.
example_sentences: Write your phone number clearly on the form.
A large number of people work from home now.

confusables.difference: Use number with things you can count: a number of students. Use amount with things you cannot count: an amount of money. A number of takes a plural verb.

entry_json.avoid: The number of students is rising takes a singular verb, but a number of students are waiting takes a plural verb.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to look after people who are ill, usually in a hospital
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My cousin works as a nurse in the local hospital and does long night shifts.
example_sentences: Nurses are in short supply in many countries.
A nurse checked my blood pressure before the doctor came in.

entry_json.definition: a small dry fruit with a hard cover that you break open before you eat it, such as a walnut or an almond
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I keep a bag of nuts in my desk for when I get hungry between classes.
example_sentences: Nuts are a good source of protein for people who do not eat meat.
Some people have a serious allergy to nuts.

entry_json.definition: a thing that you can see and touch
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The museum displays everyday objects from a hundred years ago.
example_sentences: Sharp objects are not allowed in hand luggage.
Describe an object that is important to you.
entry_json.avoid: The noun object is stressed on the first part, but the verb to object, meaning to disagree, is stressed on the second.

entry_json.definition: one of the very large areas of salt water that cover most of the Earth
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Plastic waste now reaches even the deepest parts of the ocean.
example_sentences: The Pacific is the largest ocean in the world.
Rising ocean temperatures are damaging coral reefs.

confusables.difference: An ocean is one of the five huge bodies of water. A sea is smaller and usually partly enclosed by land, such as the Mediterranean Sea.

entry_json.definition: used to show that something belongs to or is part of something else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The cost of living is the main reason young people leave the area.
example_sentences: The roof of the building was damaged in the storm.
She is a member of the running club.

confusables.difference: Of is a weak linking word said quickly as uhv. Off means away or not on, and rhymes with cough. Do not write should of; the correct form is should have.

entry_json.definition: away from a place or from the top of something, or not working
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Please switch the lights off when you leave the room.
example_sentences: He took two days off work to prepare for the exam.
The lid came off the box in the post.

entry_json.definition: to say that you are happy to give something or do something for someone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The company offered me a place on their training scheme.
example_sentences: She offered to help me with my application.
The college offers evening courses for working adults.

confusables.difference: You offer something you will provide yourself: I offered to drive. You suggest an idea for someone else to consider: I suggested taking the train.

entry_json.definition: a room or building where people work at desks
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Our office moved to a smaller building when half the staff went remote.
example_sentences: I share an office with two colleagues.
The head office is in the capital.

entry_json.definition: a person with an important job in the police, the army or the government
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A police officer explained the new parking rules to the residents.
example_sentences: The immigration officer checked my passport and visa.
She works as a training officer for a large charity.

entry_json.definition: many times; again and again
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I often cycle to work when the weather is dry.
example_sentences: People often underestimate how long the journey takes.
How often do you visit your family?
entry_json.avoid: Often goes before the main verb but after am, is or are: I often go, but I am often late.

entry_json.definition: a sound that people make when they are surprised, happy or sad
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Oh, I did not realise the deadline had already passed.
example_sentences: Oh, that is a shame.

entry_json.avoid: Oh belongs in speech only. Do not use it in Task 1 or Task 2 writing.

entry_json.definition: a thick dark material that moves like water, comes from under the ground and is burned to make cars and machines work; also the kind used in cooking
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Countries that depend on oil are trying to develop other industries.
example_sentences: Oil prices affect the cost of almost everything.
Heat a little oil in the pan before adding the vegetables.
entry_json.avoid: Oil is uncountable when you mean the substance: some oil, not an oil.

entry_json.definition: having lived or existed for a long time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The old part of the city has narrow streets and no space for cars.
example_sentences: My laptop is six years old and very slow.
Older people may need extra help with new technology.
entry_json.avoid: To give an age, say she is twenty years old or a twenty year old woman, never she has twenty years.

entry_json.definition: touching the top or the outside of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I left my notes on the kitchen table and had to go back for them.
example_sentences: The report is on my desk.
We travelled on the same train.

confusables.difference: Use on for surfaces and for days: on the wall, on Friday. Use in for enclosed spaces and longer periods: in the box, in July.

entry_json.definition: one time only, or at some time in the past
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I visit my hometown once a year, usually in the summer.
example_sentences: I have only been abroad once.
This building was once a factory.

entry_json.definition: the number 1, or a single person or thing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: One of the main reasons I moved here was the cost of housing.
example_sentences: I only have one brother.
Which one would you choose?
entry_json.avoid: One of takes a plural noun but a singular verb: one of my friends is a teacher.

entry_json.definition: a round white or brown vegetable with a strong smell and taste
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Almost every dish I cook starts with an onion and some garlic.
example_sentences: Chop the onion finely before frying it.
Onions are cheap and keep for weeks.

entry_json.definition: connected to or done using the internet
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most of my course is online, which saves me two hours of travel a day.
example_sentences: Online shopping has changed the way town centres look.
You can book the test online in a few minutes.

entry_json.definition: and no one or nothing more than that
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I only had two weeks to prepare, so I studied every evening.
example_sentences: The library is only open until six.
Only three people came to the first meeting.
entry_json.avoid: Put only just before the words it limits. I only asked her name and I asked only her name mean different things.

entry_json.definition: moving to a position on something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He stepped onto the platform just as the train doors closed.
example_sentences: The cat jumped onto the table.
Copy the file onto a memory stick.

confusables.difference: Onto shows movement to a surface: she climbed onto the roof. On shows position with no movement: she sat on the roof.

entry_json.definition: to move something so that it is no longer closed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I open the window every morning to let some fresh air in.
example_sentences: The new shopping centre opens next month.
Open your books at page twenty.

entry_json.definition: what you think or believe about something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In my opinion, public transport should be cheaper than driving.
example_sentences: Opinions about the new law are divided.
She asked for my opinion on the design.
entry_json.avoid: Say in my opinion, not according to my opinion or in my point of view.

entry_json.definition: a chance to do something that you would like to do

entry_json.definition: as different as possible from something else, or facing something across from it

entry_json.definition: one of the things you can choose

entry_json.definition: used to join two possible choices
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I usually walk or cycle to work rather than take the bus.
example_sentences: Would you like tea or coffee?
